report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Blind-spot maps: auditing what a structural equation model's design could not have detected

author.affiliation:
Institute of Information Studies
								Jagiellonian University

text.text: A structural equation model can fit its data even when the design had little chance of detecting substantively relevant alternatives.

A blind-spot map enumerates single-parameter alternatives to a fitted model, applies each at a standardized magnitude that holds implied variances fixed, and reports the probability that a stated decision rule would flag the model if the alternative were true, beside the probability that the same rule flags a correctly specified model.

Analytic detection from the noncentral chi-square is paired with a simulated path that measures each rule's finite-sample size, and equivalence that follows from a saturated latent structure is certified by proof instead of by a numerical threshold.

In ten published designs with N from 20 to 2,566, 2,035 alternatives are detectable, and all 177 admissible directed-path and latent-covariance alternatives are certified equivalent, so the fits test only the measurement structure.

Median detection under the likelihood-ratio test rises from .071 at N = 20 to .996 at N = 2,566, and the largest design still has three blind spots, residual correlations of 0.3 detected at most 9.6 percent of the time against a size of 5.8 percent.
The RMSEA > .06 rule flags 457 alternatives below .50 that the likelihood-ratio test detects above .80, and its measured size reaches .434 at N = 20.
text.formatted: The RMSEA > .06 rule flags 457 alternatives below .50 that the likelihood-ratio test detects above .80, and its measured size reaches .434 at N = 20.

text.text: A declared block of correlated residuals among reverse-keyed items is detected with probability .998 where no single pair exceeds .520.
Independent R and Julia packages generate reproducible artifacts.
Several plausible structures can fit the same observed data in a structural equation model (MacCallum, Wegener, Uchino, & Fabrigar, 1993; Raykov & Marcoulides, 2001; Stelzl, 1986).
text.formatted: Several plausible structures can fit the same observed data in a structural equation model <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(MacCallum, Wegener, Uchino, & Fabrigar, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Raykov & Marcoulides, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Stelzl, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Whether a fit decision tells the reader anything about a particular alternative depends on the analysis model, which is the model actually fitted, on the sample size, and on the decision rule that was applied.

Where a study had little power against a specified alternative, that alternative stays compatible with the reported fit, even in a case where the population covariance it implies differs from the covariance of the fitted model (Satorra & Saris, 1985).
text.formatted: Where a study had little power against a specified alternative, that alternative stays compatible with the reported fit, even in a case where the population covariance it implies differs from the covariance of the fitted model <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Satorra & Saris, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Power analysis gives the probability of detecting a specified misspecification (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996; Satorra & Saris, 1985).
text.formatted: Power analysis gives the probability of detecting a specified misspecification (MacCallum, <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Browne, & Sugawara, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Satorra & Saris, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Analytical tools and software support that calculation for a pair of models, under the likelihood-ratio test and under rules based on the RMSEA (Jak, Jorgensen, Verdam, Oort, & Elffers, 2021; Moshagen & Bader, 2024), but the competing models and their magnitudes are still selected by the analyst.
text.formatted: Analytical tools and software support that calculation for a pair of models, under the likelihood-ratio test and under rules based on the RMSEA <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Jak, Jorgensen, Verdam, Oort, & Elffers, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Moshagen & Bader, 2024)</ref>, but the competing models and their magnitudes are still selected by the analyst.

text.text: This paper proposes a blind-spot map, a report that answers the same question for a whole catalogue of competing models generated from the fitted model instead of for one pair chosen by hand.

Each entry of the catalogue frees one parameter that the fitted model holds fixed, a position referred to below as a coordinate, and sets it to a standardized magnitude under a single magnitude convention.

The entries are grouped in families, where a family consists of all the alternatives that one generating rule produces, such as every cross-loading from a factor to an indicator it does not load on, or every residual covariance between two indicators.

The catalogue exposes the covariance-equivalent alternatives as well, whose implications for structural interpretation are established in the SEM literature (MacCallum et al., 1993; Stelzl, 1986). Saris, Satorra, and van der Veld (2009) argue that overall fit indices do not indicate the size of a misspecification, and they evaluate restricted parameters one at a time with the expected parameter change, the modification index and the power of the modification-index test.
text.formatted: The catalogue exposes the covariance-equivalent alternatives as well, whose implications for structural interpretation are established in the SEM literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(MacCallum et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Stelzl, 1986)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Saris, Satorra, and van der Veld (2009)</ref> argue that overall fit indices do not indicate the size of a misspecification, and they evaluate restricted parameters one at a time with the expected parameter change, the modification index and the power of the modification-index test.

text.text: The map proposed here shares that view of the parameters.
The question it asks of them is a different one, whether the decision rule that a study applied to its overall fit could have rejected the model had a given misspecification been present.
An answer is given for every eligible coordinate in the families that the analyst declares for the run, four of which are enumerated by default.

Each coordinate carries a standardized magnitude, an admissibility status that records whether the alternative yields a proper population covariance to which the analysis model can be fitted, and a detection probability, which is the probability that the rule rejects the model when that alternative holds.

The detection probabilities of a design, reported beside the probability that the same rule rejects a correctly specified model, make up its detection profile, and an alternative whose detection lies at or near that second probability is a blind spot of the design.
Sensitivity analysis in observational research makes the effect of a specified unmeasured structure explicit (VanderWeele & Ding, 2017).
text.formatted: Sensitivity analysis in observational research makes the effect of a specified unmeasured structure explicit <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(VanderWeele & Ding, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The proposed map does the same for a specified structural alternative by evaluating the chance that the fitted SEM would be flagged if that alternative had generated the data.
Its scope is a decision rule applied to a covariance model.
The substantive interpretation therefore still depends on assumptions that lie outside the calculation of fit.

Exact covariance equivalence has an interpretation of its own, because two models that imply the same population covariance cannot be told apart by their fit at any sample size (Raykov & Marcoulides, 2001; Stelzl, 1986), whereas a positive population discrepancy leaves detection low at the available sample size and lets it rise in a larger study (MacCallum et al., 1996; Satorra & Saris, 1985).
text.formatted: Exact covariance equivalence has an interpretation of its own, because two models that imply the same population covariance cannot be told apart by their fit at any sample size <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Raykov & Marcoulides, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Stelzl, 1986)</ref>, whereas a positive population discrepancy leaves detection low at the available sample size and lets it rise in a larger study <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(MacCallum et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Satorra & Saris, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: The blind-spot map therefore keeps the two cases apart.
Where an alternative changes only the latent covariance structure and the analysis model leaves that structure saturated, the equivalence is certified by proof.
For every other entry the classification as equivalent rests on a stated numerical tolerance, and the map records which of the two bases applies.
The blind-spot map is made up of five elements.
Its enumeration is exhaustive within the declared families, and the perturbations it applies are standardized so as to preserve the implied marginal variances.
Equivalence is certified where a proof applies and classified elsewhere.
The detection probability under each stated decision rule is reported with the size of that rule, a size that is measured by simulation and never assumed.

The last element is the sample size at which an alternative would reach a chosen detection level, as in sample-size planning for a specified alternative (MacCallum et al., 1996; Moshagen & Bader, 2024).
text.formatted: The last element is the sample size at which an alternative would reach a chosen detection level, as in sample-size planning for a specified alternative <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(MacCallum et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Moshagen & Bader, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The software writes a structured file, the artifact, which records the catalogue with every quantity needed to verify its entries, and from it a reader can regenerate the catalogue and recompute any entry.
Applications in psychology frequently interpret approximate-fit indices alongside the likelihood-ratio test or in its place (Jackson, Gillaspy, & Purc-Stephenson, 2009; Ropovik, 2015).
text.formatted: Applications in psychology frequently interpret approximate-fit indices alongside the likelihood-ratio test or in its place <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Jackson, Gillaspy, & Purc-Stephenson, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Ropovik, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The operating characteristics of a fixed cutoff depend on the model and on the sample size (F. Chen, Curran, Bollen, Kirby, & Paxton, 2008; Groskurth, Bluemke, & Lechner, 2024).
text.formatted: The operating characteristics of a fixed cutoff depend on the model and on the sample size (F. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Chen, Curran, Bollen, Kirby, & Paxton, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Groskurth, Bluemke, & Lechner, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Across the detectable alternatives of the ten designs analyzed below, median detection is .239 under the likelihood-ratio test and below .001 under the RMSEA > .06 rule (Hu & Bentler, 1999), while the measured size of the RMSEA rule ranges from .434 to below .001.
text.formatted: Across the detectable alternatives of the ten designs analyzed below, median detection is .239 under the likelihood-ratio test and below .001 under the RMSEA > .06 rule <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hu & Bentler, 1999)</ref>, while the measured size of the RMSEA rule ranges from .434 to below .001.

text.text: Model-specific calibration of the cutoffs offers another route to stated error rates (McNeish & Wolf, 2023).
text.formatted: Model-specific calibration of the cutoffs offers another route to stated error rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(McNeish & Wolf, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The blind-spot map complements that route by reporting the detection of each declared alternative once a rule is specified. Pesigan, Cheung, Wu, Chang, and Leung (2026) also generate a set of neighboring models from the fitted model, and they weigh the plausibility of each given the observed data by a Bayesian posterior probability computed from the Bayesian information criterion.
text.formatted: The blind-spot map complements that route by reporting the detection of each declared alternative once a rule is specified. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Pesigan, Cheung, Wu, Chang, and Leung (2026)</ref> also generate a set of neighboring models from the fitted model, and they weigh the plausibility of each given the observed data by a Bayesian posterior probability computed from the Bayesian information criterion.

text.text: The two approaches are complementary in that posterior probabilities compare the alternatives in the light of the data in hand, whereas the blind-spot map states how often the decision rule of the design would have rejected the fitted model under each alternative.
The latter is a frequency property of the design, and it holds before the data are consulted.
Neither probability is a verdict on whether a published model or any competing model generated the observed data.

A blind-spot map is a falsifier and not a verifier, in the sense that it can show that a design could not have distinguished the fitted model from a stated alternative and can never show that the fitted model is correct.
Applied to ten published designs, the proposed map shows three properties that a fit statistic does not reveal.

In every design with latent variables the covariance evidence bears on the measurement structure alone, because all directed paths and latent covariances among the factors are certified equivalent (Lee & Hershberger, 1990; Stelzl, 1986).
text.formatted: In every design with latent variables the covariance evidence bears on the measurement structure alone, because all directed paths and latent covariances among the factors are certified equivalent <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lee & Hershberger, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Stelzl, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: The actual size of the likelihood-ratio test departs from its nominal level in the three smallest designs, by amounts that the asymptotic theory does not show and that small samples lead one to expect (Curran, Bollen, Paxton, Kirby, & Chen, 2002; Moshagen, 2012).
text.formatted: The actual size of the likelihood-ratio test departs from its nominal level in the three smallest designs, by amounts that the asymptotic theory does not show and that small samples lead one to expect <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Curran, Bollen, Paxton, Kirby, & Chen, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Moshagen, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The RMSEA cutoff leaves almost every enumerated alternative unflagged, which is a property of the rule that a sensitivity statement can make explicit.
The analysis model is written in reticular action notation (McArdle & McDonald, 1984).
text.formatted: The analysis model is written in reticular action notation <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(McArdle & McDonald, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: The directed coefficients are held in an asymmetric matrix A and the variances and covariances in a symmetric matrix S, while a selection picks the observed indices out of the m modeled variables.
With E = (I -A) -1 , the implied covariance of the p observed variables is the observed submatrix of ESE ′ , written Σ(θ) for a free parameter vector θ.

Because reticular action notation represents directed paths, residual covariances and mean structures in one algebra (McArdle & McDonald, 1984), one perturbation mechanism reaches every family of alternatives that the map enumerates.

An alternative is a single competing model, obtained by freeing one parameter of the analysis model at one coordinate and setting that parameter to one magnitude.
The catalogue is the enumerated set of alternatives for a fitted model.
A family is the set of alternatives that one generating rule produces.

Four families are enumerated in every design, the first being a cross-loading from a latent variable to an indicator outside its analysis-model indicators and the second a residual covariance between two observed variables whose residuals are uncorrelated in the analysis model.

Cross-loadings are often observed in applications and frequently disregarded, and omitting one that exists in the population biases the loadings and the structural parameters of the fitted model (Navarro & Schermelleh-Engel, 2025).

text.text: A covariance between two latent variables that the analysis model leaves uncorrelated forms the third family, and a directed path between latent variables where none is specified forms the fourth.

text.text: The convention adopted here is that a perturbation of standardized magnitude m is applied together with an adjustment to the corresponding residual variance that holds the implied marginal variances of the observed variables at their fitted values.

Without the adjustment, adding a cross-loading inflates the variance of the affected indicator, and the design then detects a mixture of the structural change and the variance change, in proportions that differ from cell to cell.

The derivation of the adjustment is given in Appendix A. A loading that differs between groups is scaled in the same way within the group concerned, and a declared alternative applies all its components before the residual variances are adjusted once.

The marginal-variance adjustment requires positive residual variances, and an adjusted residual variance at or below zero gives the status inadmissible_dgp at the declared magnitude, in which case the entry retains its magnitude and receives no detection probability.

The covariance check prevents a transcription error from becoming a silent change of the model.

The extractor also refuses every fit whose test statistic the analytic map does not model, which covers inequality constraints and bounds, robust test statistics (Satorra & Bentler, 2001), estimators other than maximum likelihood, ordered indicators (Muthén, 1984), sampling weights, multilevel structure, constrained mean structures, and full-information likelihood on incomplete cases (Enders & Bandalos, 2001), and each refusal names its reason.

In both packages the refit of the analysis model to a perturbed covariance runs a scaled quasi-Newton search, followed by a second optimizer started from its result, keeps the lower discrepancy, and accepts it only at a stationary point.

Verification is reported at one of three levels, and a verifier states which one it used.

Structural verification confirms that the artifact parses, that its dimensions are consistent and that its digests recompute, and it regenerates the auto-generated part of the catalogue exactly from the recorded rule.
The structural level needs no raw data and still catches a narrowed catalogue.
Statistical verification recomputes every analytic value, which has to agree within 10 -6 , and reruns the simulated values from the recorded seed with either package.
A rerun value is accepted when it lies within z 1-0.01/(2k) combined Monte Carlo standard errors of the recorded one, where k counts the simulated alternatives and the calibration run.
The whole artifact is thereby held to a family-wise error rate of one percent.
Exact verification reruns the artifact with the package, the version and the platform that produced it and requires bit-identical output.
A simulated artifact records the package, its version and the platform.
The verifier checks these three before it compares outputs bit for bit, whereas comparisons across packages and platforms use the statistical tier (Appendix D).
All ten corpus artifacts validate against the JSON Schema of the format, regenerate their catalogues exactly and pass structural verification in both packages.
Each package also verifies the artifacts of the other at the statistical tier (Section 4).

Validation compares the numerical components with lavaan, with independent power calculations, with direct refits to population covariances and with simulated rejection rates, and it compares the two packages with each other, so that the comparisons establish together the numerical accuracy and the finite-sample limits of the reported probabilities.

Five comparisons with independent implementations assess the discrepancy, the power calculation, the rejection behavior that the map predicts and the simulated path, and the last of them compares the two packages with each other.

The third anchor tests the claim that the map makes, with data generated from a planted alternative, a cross-loading at standardized magnitude 0.20 with F M = 0.0629 at N = 150 on eight degrees of freedom, to which the analysis model was fitted in 4,000 independent samples.
The map predicted a detection probability of .554 and the observed rejection rate was .548, a difference of 0.74 Monte Carlo standard errors.

The same test confirms that the map points at the right coordinate, because among the 58 admissible alternatives in that catalogue the planted one is the unique nearest entry to the generating covariance, at a discrepancy of zero against a runner-up of 0.152.

The fourth anchor compares the simulated path with an independent simulation, in which replications were drawn in four designs spanning N = 20 to N = 403 from the fitted model and from three alternatives and were refitted with the R package and, separately, with lavaan, 4,000 replications each.

Across the 16 conditions the two rejection rates of the likelihood-ratio test differ by at most 2.02 combined Monte Carlo standard errors, and the rates of the RMSEA rule by about one percentage point at most.

Under the fitted model the two implementations agree on sizes between .065 and .098 in the designs with N = 20, N = 75 and N = 403, so that the finite-sample departures described in Section 5.3 are properties of the designs and do not arise from either program.
The fifth anchor compares the two packages, which share no code.

Mapping the ten corpus designs from the same fitted models, they assign the same status to all 2,583 entries and the same basis to every equivalent one, and their analytic detection probabilities differ by at most 1.7 × 10 -11 .

Their simulated detection probabilities are drawn from different random streams, and over the 2,098 entries that both packages simulate, five standardized differences exceed three in absolute value, against 5.7 expected by chance, the largest being 3.35.

Starting instead from the raw data or the published moments, the Julia package fits the ten models itself and recovers the parameter structure of lavaan in all ten of them, with estimates within a relative 3.9 × 10 -6 of those of lavaan and analytic detection within 5.7 × 10 -6 of the R map.
Each package verifies the ten artifacts of the other at the structural and at the statistical tier.
Five invariants are checked across the entries of the catalogue.

Multiplying an indicator by a positive constant and refitting must leave every detection probability unchanged, since a standardized magnitude cannot depend on the arbitrary units of an indicator, and reordering the variables must leave the map unchanged up to relabeling, because a dependence on order indicates an indexing error.

The tests check that detection does not decrease across the declared magnitude grid of each coordinate or across sample sizes for a fixed alternative, and that a zero magnitude returns the size of the rule.
Every entry that the software certifies as equivalent by Proposition 2 must also return F M < 10 -10 from the optimizer, so that the proof and the numerics check each other.

text.text: 5 Ten published models
The corpus contains the ten published model designs in table 1.
They span sample sizes of 20 to 2,566, five to seventeen observed variables, and 2 to 113 degrees of freedom, and include one non-recursive specification.

Each uses a published covariance matrix or publicly distributed raw data, cited to its origin and, where a package redistributes it, to that package (Fox, Nie, & Byrnes, 2024; R Core Team, 2025; Revelle, 2026; Rosseel, 2012).

text.text: All 18 latent-covariance alternatives and 159 of the 192 structural-path alternatives are covariance-equivalent to their analysis models, and the software certifies every one of the 177 by Proposition 2, while the other 33 structural paths are inadmissible.

The certificate applies because each of the nine designs with latent variables leaves its latent covariance structure saturated, seven of them being confirmatory factor models with freely correlated factors and two being structural models whose latent part is a complete recursive system.
In all nine, the covariance evidence bears on the measurement structure and on nothing else.

No fit statistic from these designs, at any sample size, could have distinguished a directed path between latent variables from a correlation, or one direction from another (Lee & Hershberger, 1990; Stelzl, 1986).

text.text: The map makes this explicit in every artifact instead of leaving it to a reader to notice.
The remaining nine equivalent entries carry a numerical basis and all belong to the alienation design, in which each factor has two indicators.
They are the residual covariances between the two indicators of the same factor, at three magnitudes.

Freeing such a covariance alongside the factor's loading and variance leaves the model unidentified, with a singular expected information matrix, so the analysis model absorbs the perturbation exactly.
The 63 alternatives with an improper minimizer, 60 of them cross-loadings, mark misspecifications that drive the analysis model to a negative variance in the population (Kolenikov & Bollen, 2012).

Their simulated detection has a median of .713 and ranges from .093 to one, so that a misspecification strong enough to produce a population Heywood case is usually detected, although not always.
Table 2 reports the measured size of each rule beside its analytic value.

The likelihood-ratio test rejects a correctly specified model 8.9 percent of the time in the food-market design (N = 20), 10.2 percent in the political-democracy design (N = 75) and 7.5 percent in the ability design (N = 145), and each of these rates departs from .05 by more than three Monte Carlo standard errors, as small samples and large covariance matrices lead one to expect (Curran et al., 2002; Moshagen, 2012).

The big-five items have six response categories, and the ordinal generator, which cuts normal variables at the observed category proportions, gives a size of 6.6 percent for that design.

Discreteness alone therefore accounts for little of the inflation, which comes from the joint distribution of the responses, as nonnormal data inflate the normal-theory statistic of a correctly specified model (Curran, West, & Finch, 1996).

text.text: In the three flagged designs the median absolute difference is .044, .062 and .039, in the quality-of-life design it is .036, and in the other six designs it is at most .013.
Pooled over the corpus, median detection is .239 analytically and .278 by simulation.
For a small design the analytic value understates how often the stated rule rejects, and the measured size shows that much of the difference consists of false positives instead of added sensitivity.

text.text: Each simulated value rests on 2,000 replications from the alternative's population covariance, with a Monte Carlo standard error of at most .011, and color encodes sample size.

Points well above the identity line are alternatives that the stated rule rejects more often than the asymptotic approximation predicts, and nearly all of them come from the three smallest designs and from the design with seventeen observed variables, whose measured sizes all exceed .05.
Residual-covariance detection tracks sample size across the ten designs, as the noncentrality λ = (N -1)F M implies for single-element perturbations of similar size.
The Spearman correlation between log N and the median analytic detection is .964 at standardized magnitude 0.2 and .952 at 0.3.
Cross-loading detection tracks N less closely, with correlations of .62 and .47, because a cross-loading's effect also depends on how many indicators its factor carries.
A residual covariance changes one off-diagonal element of the implied covariance.
A cross-loading from factor f to indicator j changes the covariances of y j with every indicator of f , so the affected block widens with the number of indicators per factor.

Across the nine designs that contain both families, the Spearman correlation between mean indicators per factor and the log ratio of median F M for cross-loadings to residual covariances is .80 at magnitude 0.3 (p = .009) and .67 at 0.2 (p = .051).
Residual covariances have the larger median F M only in designs with at most three indicators per factor, and every design with more than three has the cross-loading median ahead.
The ordering of median detection follows the same pattern without being uniform, with cross-loadings leading in seven of nine designs at magnitude 0.2 and in six of nine at 0.3.
The health-care design has the largest reversal, with median cross-loading F M between a quarter and a fifth of the residual-covariance median.

Its four factors are the most strongly correlated in the corpus, with a mean absolute correlation of .81, which is consistent with a cross-loading onto a nearly collinear factor being largely absorbed by the indicator's own loading.
Because the two families' magnitudes are standardized on different scales (Appendix A), these comparisons describe the corpus instead of a general ranking of the families.
Modification indices can localize a residual association after model rejection (Saris et al., 2009; Sörbom, 1989).

text.text: The cutoff behaves as it was built to behave, in that its rejection region tolerates population misfit below an RMSEA of .06.
The population RMSEA of the corpus alternatives, F M /df, has a median of .021 and exceeds .06 for only 2.4 percent of them.

The comparison therefore turns on a substantive choice instead of a statistical defect, the choice being whether a residual correlation of .3, or a cross-loading of .3, is a misspecification that a study may leave unflagged.
A design reported only with the cutoff makes that choice implicitly.

The map makes it explicit, alternative by alternative, and pairs each rule with its size, because fixed cutoffs have model-and sample-dependent operating characteristics (F. Chen et al., 2008; Groskurth et al., 2024; Marsh et al., 2004; Savalei, 2012).

In the big-five design at N = 2,566, the median residual correlation of 0.3 is detected with probability near one, yet the three weakest are detected 6.1, 9.5 and 9.6 percent of the time against a size of 5.8 percent.

These numbers describe how often each model would be flagged if the stated residual association generated the data.

A blind-spot map is a falsifier and not a verifier, in the sense that it shows which alternatives these designs could not have distinguished from the fitted models and supplies no evidence that any of these associations exists in the published data or that the fitted models are correct.
The worked example maps the mental-ability model of Holzinger and Swineford (1939), with nine indicators on three correlated factors at N = 301, from the raw data that lavaan distributes.

text.text: In R the model syntax and the data go to a single function, which fits the model with lavaan, enumerates the catalogue, computes the analytic map and, with simulate = TRUE, runs the simulated path with 2,000 replications for the fitted model and for every alternative.
hs <-lavaan::HolzingerSwineford1939 map <-blindspot(model, data = hs, likelihood = "wishart", simulate = TRUE) summary(map) bsm_write(map, "hs.bsm.json")

text.text: The catalogue has 180 entries, of which 144 are detectable.

The summary opens with the measured calibration, in which the likelihood-ratio test rejects the fitted model itself in 5.2 percent of the replications, with a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.5 points.
The asymptotic approximation is therefore adequate for this design, and the analytic and simulated values below agree closely.
Run with a single worker process, threads = 1, the call takes about 16 minutes on a laptop.
The artifact it writes holds the map, the calibration and the seed from which the simulated values can be rerun.
Three entries of the map illustrate the three outcomes of Fig 1.

Among the thirty-six residual covariances at standardized magnitude 0.1, the weakest, between x4 and x5, has analytic detection .052 and simulated detection .057 against a measured size of .052, which means that a residual association at that coordinate would lead to rejection about as often as a correctly specified model does.

Cross-loadings at magnitude 0.3 have a median detection of .565 and range from .263 to almost one across twelve detectable indicatorfactor pairs, while three more are inadmissible at that magnitude and three have an improper minimizer.

All eighteen directed paths between the factors are certified equivalent, because the model leaves the three factor covariances free, so that the fit carries no information about direction among the factors.
The planning functions of Section 2.8 turn the weakest entries into statements about the design.

A residual correlation of 0.2 at the median coordinate has F M = 0.0214, for which bsm_n_for_detection returns N = 1,053 for detection .80 under the likelihood-ratio test, three and a half times the sample of the study, and the weakest residual correlation of 0.1 would need about 60,000 observations.

At the sample size of the study, bsm_min_detectable(map, target = 0.8) searches each coordinate for the smallest magnitude with detection .80, which lies between 0.30 and 0.49 for 28 of the 36 residual covariances and between 0.20 and 0.42 for nine of the 18 cross-loading coordinates, whereas the other coordinates leave the admissible range of the magnitude convention before they reach it and the six directed paths are equivalent at every magnitude.

Measurement invariance is usually assessed in configural, metric and scalar steps before groups are compared (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016; Vandenberg & Lance, 2000), and the metric step, which holds the loadings equal across groups, is part of the analysis model only when the model is fitted to the groups separately.

text.text: The multi-group fit, with n = 156 and n = 145, keeps the 54 degrees of freedom that lavaan reports for it, and its catalogue contains, besides the four families in each group, 12 alternatives that raise one constrained loading in the Grant-White school by a standardized 0.1 or 0.2.

Of these, 11 are admissible, with analytic detection between .053 and .068 at 0.1 and between .060 and .159 at 0.2, so that a loading differing between the two schools by these amounts would have left the fit of the invariant model almost unaffected.

Simulated detection exceeds the analytic value by 1.4 to 3.2 points for every one of them, an excess of the order of the measured size under the fitted model, .064 with a Monte Carlo standard error of .0055, which reflects the calibration of the test in groups of about 150 and adds no sensitivity to the loadings.
When the raw data are available, the calibration can also be measured under the distribution of the data themselves, with the bootstrap generator of Section 2.7 in place of the Wishart draw.
Section 5.3 reports the result for this design and for the three other designs whose data are distributed.
bsm_simulate(map, ids = character(0), generator = "bootstrap", data = hs)

The Julia package maps the same design without R. It reads the model syntax and the data from a file, here written from R with write.csv(hs, "hs.csv", row.names = FALSE), fits the model itself, and the last line of the following code verifies the artifact that R wrote, recomputing every analytic value and rerunning the simulated ones from the recorded seed.
The 180 entries of the Julia map carry the statuses of the R map, and their analytic detection probabilities agree with those of R within 2.6 × 10 -6 .
The simulated values are drawn from the random streams of Julia.
Over the 151 entries that both packages simulate they differ from those of R by at most 3.03 combined Monte Carlo standard errors, and with a single thread the Julia call takes about 2 minutes.
A report of this fit can therefore state which misspecifications its design could plausibly have caught, which it could not, and what it would have taken to catch them.
Each of these statements can be checked by a reader against the artifact with either package.
A blind-spot map reports the probability of rejecting a fitted model under a specified alternative, at a specified magnitude and sample size and under a specified decision rule.
A blind-spot map is a falsifier, not a verifier.
It can show that a design could not have distinguished the fitted model from a stated alternative, and it can never show that the fitted model is correct.

High detection across the declared catalogue shows that the design could have rejected the model under those alternatives and supplies no probability that the model is true, so that a fitting model remains one explanation among the structures compatible with the data (MacCallum et al., 1993; Raykov & Marcoulides, 2001; Stelzl, 1986).

A sensitivity statement, of the kind that observational research reports for unmeasured confounding (Van-derWeele & Ding, 2017), can report three things beside a fit decision.

text.text: The first is the set of alternatives whose detection lies near the measured size of the rule, and the second the families that the analysis model cannot distinguish at any sample size.
The third is the sample size at which a substantively relevant alternative would reach a chosen detection level.
A sample large enough to detect an omitted cross-loading is a planning requirement that has been stated for nonlinear structural models as well (Navarro & Schermelleh-Engel, 2025).

Together they tie a reported fit decision to the alternatives that the design could and could not have examined, in a form that a reviewer can check against the artifact.
Two checks from the corpus apply to any submitted model and need no new data.

If the analysis model leaves its latent covariance structure saturated, as all nine latent-variable designs here do, its fit supports no directional claim among the latent variables (Lee & Hershberger, 1990; Stelzl, 1986), and the map certifies this property instead of leaving it to inspection.

Applied across a larger corpus, in the manner of earlier audits of published applications (MacCallum et al., 1993; Ropovik, 2015), the same catalogue rule could summarize the share of enumerated alternatives with high detection in a body of research, and the ten designs of the present corpus illustrate the quantities that such a study would need, including the size of the rule and the admissibility status of each entry.

Detection probabilities are comparable within a family under the stated standardized-magnitude convention.
Across families equal nominal magnitudes are standardized on different scales (Appendix A) and change different numbers of covariance elements, as Section 5.4 shows.

The population RMSEA (Browne & Cudeck, 1992) reported with every detectable alternative places all families on one scale of misfit, although that scale is itself insensitive to some omitted cross-loadings and to clusters of correlated residuals (Savalei, 2012), and ordering the alternatives by it would produce a different ranking that answers a different substantive question.

text.text: Proposition 2 Let the analysis model satisfy three conditions. (i) No directed path leaves an observed variable, and no observed residual covaries with a latent variable. (ii) Every observed residual variance and every latent variance or disturbance variance is free. (iii) The latent variables can be ordered so that the exogenous ones come first, every pair of exogenous latent variables is joined by a free covariance, every other pair is joined by exactly one free directed path from the earlier to the later variable, and no other latent coefficient or covariance is free or fixed at a nonzero value.

Let an alternative change only latent coefficients or latent covariances, let its latent covariance matrix Ψ ′ be positive definite, and let the residual variances of the observed variables be adjusted, as in Appendix A, to positive values that hold the observed variances at their fitted values.
Then Σ A belongs to the covariance set of the analysis model, and F M = 0 at every sample size.

Proof Under (i) the implied covariance is ΛΨΛ ′ + Θ, where Λ holds the loadings, Θ the observed residual covariances, and Ψ = (I -B) -1 Φ(I -B) -⊤ , with B strictly lower triangular in the ordering of (iii) and Φ block diagonal, with a free block for the exogenous latent variables and free disturbance variances for the others, and every positive definite Ψ ′ has this form.

To obtain it, the exogenous block of Φ is set to the corresponding block of Ψ ′ , and then, for each endogenous latent variable in turn, the population regression on all preceding latent variables within Ψ ′ supplies the free coefficients in its row of B, while its residual variance, positive because Ψ ′ is positive definite, supplies its disturbance variance.
The alternative leaves Λ and the off-diagonal elements of Θ unchanged and alters only diagonal elements of Θ, which are free by (ii).
Hence Σ A = ΛΨ ′ Λ ′ + Θ ′ is the implied covariance at an admissible parameter value, and the minimum of F ML is zero.
□ Confirmatory factor models with freely correlated factors and marker indicators satisfy the conditions, as do structural models whose latent part is a complete recursive system.
Every corpus design with latent variables is of one of these two kinds.
